findings.title: Stop executing an unpinned remote installer in the image build
findings.whyItBreaks: The new RUN downloads https://example.com/install.sh at build time and pipes it to sh as root, with no checksum, signature, version pin, or pinned-digest artifact. curl -L follows redirects to whatever that URL (or a later hop) returns, and the bytes are executed in the build and baked into the image that CMD ["/app"] ships. This is unsigned remote code execution on every build, including after a CDN/DNS/host compromise or a 3xx to a different origin.

findings.title: Fail the RUN when the installer fetch fails
findings.whyItBreaks: curl is invoked without --fail, with -s (stderr muted, no -S), in a pipe whose status is sh's, not curl's (POSIX/ash default; no set -o pipefail). HTTP 4xx/5xx still exit 0 and feed the body to sh. A transport failure leaves sh with empty stdin, which exits 0, so Docker commits the layer. COPY/CMD then proceed as if the install succeeded; failed install and successful install are indistinguishable.

findings.title: Stop executing unpinned remote install.sh in the image build
findings.whyItBreaks: The new RUN fetches https://example.com/install.sh and pipes it into sh as root while building the runtime image (COPY app /app; CMD ["/app"]). Nothing pins a digest, signature, or even an immutable URL, so whatever that host returns is executed and baked into the artifact (supply-chain RCE at build). curl is invoked with -s and without --fail, and the pipeline runs under Alpine /bin/sh -c with pipefail off, so a network error or non-2xx body does not fail the layer: curl's status is discarded, sh reads empty or HTML stdin, and a successful empty sh exits 0 — the image still ships, indistinguishable from a real install.

findings.title: Stop piping an unpinned remote installer into sh
findings.whyItBreaks: The added layer runs `curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh` as root at image build. There is no digest, signature, version pin, or `--fail`, and `-L` follows redirects, so the live response body is executed as the build user. Fetching that URL returns the IANA Example Domain HTML page (not an installer), so the build either runs untrusted markup as shell or fails nondeterministically; a later redirect or content change is executed with no review. That is remote code execution of the shippable image.

findings.title: Fail the build when the installer download fails
findings.whyItBreaks: Docker's default SHELL is `/bin/sh -c` with no `pipefail`. The pipeline's exit status is only `sh`'s. `curl -s` mutes curl errors and does not pass `--fail`, so a transport failure yields empty stdin, `sh` exits 0, and the layer is cached as success; an HTTP 4xx/5xx body is likewise executed because curl still exits 0. Subsequent `COPY`/`CMD` then ship an image that did not run the intended installer, with no distinguishable failure.

findings.title: Stop discarding Load errors in exported LoadOrDefault
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ("", ErrMissing) when a key is absent and ("", nil) when the key is present with an empty value. LoadOrDefault is exported and binds that error to _, always returning the string. Callers of this public API cannot tell failure from a real empty value, so a missing key is observed as a legitimate "".

findings.title: Propagate Load's error from exported LoadOrDefault
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ("", ErrMissing) when the key is absent and ("", nil) when the key is present with an empty value. LoadOrDefault is an exported wrapper that binds the error to `_` and returns only the string, so missing-key failure and a legitimate empty value are the same result. Every caller of this public API is forced to persist, display, or otherwise act on "" as if the lookup succeeded.

findings.title: Do not discard Load errors in public LoadOrDefault
findings.whyItBreaks: Exported LoadOrDefault ignores Load's error return. Load yields ("", ErrMissing) when the key is absent and ("", nil) when the key is present with an empty value; the wrapper returns "" for both, so callers cannot tell failure from a real empty string. Any other Load error would also be dropped.

findings.title: Wait for worker goroutines before Run returns
findings.whyItBreaks: The loop still processes every job, but each `results <- j * 2` now runs in a detached goroutine and Run returns as soon as the spawns finish. Previously the sends were synchronous, so returning from Run meant every result had been delivered. Callers that then close(results) — the normal way to unblock `for range results` — race those sends and panic with 'send on closed channel'. Callers that treat return as completion can also observe fewer than len(jobs) values. Channel sends from the goroutines are themselves safe; the defect is the lost completion barrier.

findings.title: Wait for worker goroutines before Run returns
findings.whyItBreaks: Run previously sent every j*2 on results and only then returned, so callers could close(results) or treat return as completion. The new goroutines are not waited on, so Run returns immediately after launch. The standard pattern `Run(...); close(results)` (or `go func(){ Run(...); close(results) }()` plus `range results`) can close the channel while sends are still in flight, panicking with send on closed channel. Even without close, a caller cannot tell when all jobs have been written, so a buffered drain after Run can miss results. Loop-variable capture is correct; the defect is missing join.

findings.title: Wait for spawned job goroutines before Run returns
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously Run sent every `j*2` (or blocked on send) before returning, so return was a completion barrier. The new loop only starts `len(jobs)` goroutines and falls off the end of Run with no WaitGroup/errgroup. Callers that close `results` after Run returns can panic on send-on-closed-channel; callers that inspect a buffered `results` immediately after return can observe a partial batch. Goroutines still blocked on `results <-` after the receiver stops are leaked, and `ctx` is never selected so cancellation cannot join or unblock them.

findings.title: Revert canDeleteRecord OR that bypasses admin and tenant checks
findings.whyItBreaks: The delete gate changed from session.isAdmin && same-tenant to ||. Substituting live Session/RecordRef shapes: (isAdmin=false, tenantId match) is now true, so any same-tenant user may delete any record; (isAdmin=true, other tenant) is now true, so an admin may delete another tenant's records. Previously both were false. ownerId/userId are unused, so this is not owner-scoped delete — it is an authorization bypass of the previous admin+tenant policy.

findings.title: Restore tenant-scoped admin check; || allows unauthorized deletes
findings.whyItBreaks: canDeleteRecord previously required both session.isAdmin and session.tenantId === record.tenantId. The || change authorizes two previously denied cases: (1) a non-admin in the same tenant can delete any record in that tenant; (2) an admin whose session.tenantId does not match record.tenantId can delete across tenants. Session still carries a tenantId, so isAdmin is a tenant-bound flag; the only extra power || gives isAdmin is cross-tenant delete. RecordRef.ownerId is unused, so this is not an owner-or-admin check either.

findings.title: Revert canDeleteRecord to require admin and tenant match
findings.whyItBreaks: Base required session.isAdmin && session.tenantId === record.tenantId, so only a same-tenant admin could delete. The new || is a superset: (1) isAdmin=true with tenantId 'A' vs record.tenantId 'B' now returns true (cross-tenant admin delete); (2) isAdmin=false with matching tenantId now returns true (any tenant member can delete any record in that tenant). RecordRef.ownerId is still unused, so this is not an owner-or-admin check. The function is the exported authorization contract.

findings.title: Propagate parseSettings failures instead of returning DEFAULTS
findings.whyItBreaks: The new catch-all maps JSON.parse SyntaxError and the in-body Error("bad theme")/Error("bad fontSize") throws to `{ theme: "light", fontSize: 14 }`, which is identical to legitimate default settings. parseSettings is exported, so callers cannot tell failed parse from valid input. The in-repo caller updateFontSize (src/settings.ts:20-22) previously aborted before save(); now it mutates fontSize on the fallback and save()s, e.g. updateFontSize('{"theme":"dark"}', 18, save) writes {"theme":"light","fontSize":18} and drops the original theme.

findings.title: Stop swallowing parseSettings failures as DEFAULTS
findings.whyItBreaks: The new catch-all converts JSON.parse failures and this function's own validation throws ("bad theme" / "bad fontSize") into `{theme:"light", fontSize:14}`. Callers can no longer tell failure from a legitimate default document. Live caller updateFontSize always writes that object: e.g. raw `{"theme":"dark"}` (valid theme, missing/non-number fontSize) previously threw and skipped save; now save() persists `{"theme":"light","fontSize":<size>}`, silently dropping the original theme. Same overwrite happens for malformed JSON and for `{"theme":"dark","fontSize":"16"}`.

findings.title: Stop mapping parseSettings failures onto DEFAULTS
findings.whyItBreaks: The new empty catch converts JSON.parse SyntaxError, Error("bad theme"), Error("bad fontSize"), and any other throw into `{ theme: "light", fontSize: 14 }`, which is indistinguishable from a real settings object. updateFontSize always assigns fontSize and calls save, so invalid raw that previously aborted now persists defaults plus the new size and wipes theme.

When 0 < totalItems < pageSize, it returns 0 instead of 1, reporting no pages for a non-empty list. Exact multiples (pageCount(9, 3) === 3) still look correct, which hides the regression.

findings.title: Fetch artifacts from the branch commit, not ref("verified")
findings.whyItBreaks: buildReport still sets builtFrom from build.ref(branch) but now loads artifacts via build.ref("verified"). Whenever those refs resolve to different commits (any branch other than "verified", or a verified pointer that has moved), the returned BuildReport claims a branch commit while listing another commit's artifacts. Callers have no way to detect the mismatch.

findings.title: Load artifacts from the same commit as builtFrom
findings.whyItBreaks: buildReport still sets builtFrom from build.ref(branch) but now calls artifactsAt(build.ref("verified")). When branch is not the verified ref, the returned report attributes another commit's artifacts to the branch commit. That is a behavior change on the exported API: callers receive a structurally valid but internally inconsistent BuildReport.

findings.title: Stop pairing branch builtFrom with verified-ref artifacts
findings.whyItBreaks: buildReport still sets builtFrom from build.ref(branch) but now loads artifacts via build.ref("verified"). When those refs resolve to different SHAs, the report attributes another commit's artifacts to the branch commit. Previously both fields used the same commit, so this is a silent mismatch in the exported report.

findings.title: Restore slice so recentEntries still caps at limit
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported JSDoc still promises at most `limit` entries, but the new body only special-cases `limit <= 0` and otherwise returns the full reversed copy. `renderFeed` calls `recentEntries(all, 20)` then copies `page.length` into the result, so a feed longer than 20 items is emitted in full instead of a 20-entry page.

findings.title: Restore the `limit` cap in recentEntries
findings.whyItBreaks: JSDoc and the public `limit` parameter promise at most `limit` entries. The body now returns the full reversed copy whenever `limit > 0`. renderFeed always passes 20, allocates a 20-slot array, then copies `page.length` items — so a feed longer than 20 grows `out` and returns every entry instead of a 20-item page.

findings.title: Cap recentEntries at `limit` after the slice was dropped
findings.whyItBreaks: JSDoc and the `limit` parameter still promise at most `limit` entries. The old body reversed then `.slice(0, limit)`. The new body returns the entire reversed copy whenever `limit > 0`. `renderFeed` calls `recentEntries(all, 20)` and copies `page.length` into a 20-slot array; assigning past index 19 grows that array, so a feed longer than 20 now returns every reversed entry.

findings.title: Keep entry-count aligned with filtered live rows
findings.whyItBreaks: renderManifest now drops stale entries from the body (`live`) but still passes `entries.length` to `headerLines`, which emits `# entry-count: ${count}`. Before this change, count always equaled the number of data rows. After it, a mix of stale and live entries produces a header count larger than the listed rows. `renderManifest` is exported public API, so callers that size, parse, or validate the manifest from `# entry-count` observe a truncated/corrupt body relative to the promised count.

findings.title: Align # entry-count with live rows after stale filter
findings.whyItBreaks: renderManifest now omits stale entries from the body but still passes entries.length into headerLines. `# entry-count` previously matched the number of data rows; with any stale=true entry it now over-reports (e.g. 2 entries, 1 stale → `# entry-count: 2` and one path/size row). Parsers or tools that trust the header count will over-count, wait for missing rows, or treat omitted stale files as present.

findings.title: Sync # entry-count with filtered live rows
findings.whyItBreaks: Rows are built from live = entries.filter(!e.stale), but headerLines still receives entries.length. # entry-count therefore overstates the number of path/size lines whenever any entry is stale, breaking the previous invariant that the header count equals the body row count (headerLines interpolates count at line 15 into the returned public string).

findings.title: Keep token check returning False on non-str stored_hash
findings.whyItBreaks: `hmac.compare_digest` raises TypeError when `stored_hash` is None, bytes, or otherwise not the same type as `token_hash()`'s hex str (or is a non-ASCII str). The previous `==` returned False, so `guard` returned `{"status": 401}` and did not run `handler`. After this change those inputs escape `guard` as an uncaught exception instead of a deny.

findings.title: Restore execute() so it returns the uppercased input
findings.whyItBreaks: execute() is the repo's only public API and is typed to return string. The body now unconditionally throws Error("always fails"), so every caller that previously received input.toUpperCase() now gets an exception instead of a result. That is an unusable core path, not a narrowed edge case.

findings.title: Restore execute to return the uppercased input
findings.whyItBreaks: execute is the module's only public API and is typed to return a string. The body now unconditionally throws Error("always fails"), so every caller fails instead of receiving input.toUpperCase().

findings.title: Stop throwing from execute; restore the string result
findings.whyItBreaks: Public execute(input: string): string previously returned input.toUpperCase(). The body now always throws Error('always fails'), so every caller gets an exception instead of a string and the module's only export is unusable.

findings.title: Stop rejecting viewers in isEligible; it blocks read-only
findings.whyItBreaks: isEligible now returns false when req.role === "viewer". handle() is the only caller and treats !isEligible as "rejected" before the existing viewer branch that returns "read-only". Precondition substitution: role="viewer", status="active", attempts<5 → !isEligible @src/handler.ts:24 is true → "rejected"; the read-only action @src/handler.ts:25 is unreachable. That path was independently approvable (active + under attempt cap); the new role gate does not legitimately govern it.

findings.title: Do not reject viewers in isEligible; it blocks read-only handle
findings.whyItBreaks: isEligible now returns false when req.role === "viewer". handle is the only call site and uses that result as a hard reject before role routing. An active viewer with attempts < 5 previously passed isEligible and received "read-only" at src/handler.ts:25; the same request now returns "rejected". The viewer branch is unreachable. Admin/editor paths are unchanged because they are not viewers; the new predicate therefore only over-blocks the distinct read-only action it does not govern.

findings.title: Do not reject viewers in shared isEligible gate
findings.whyItBreaks: handle() treats isEligible as a shared precondition, then dispatches three distinct outcomes by role: viewer→"read-only", admin→"elevated", editor→"processed". The new `req.role === "viewer"` clause makes isEligible return false for every viewer, so handle short-circuits to "rejected" at line 24 and the viewer success path at line 25 is unreachable. An active viewer with attempts < 5 was legitimately approvable for read-only independently of this role check; substituting role="viewer" into the new guard produces a wrong rejection.

findings.title: Shared canProceed payment gate over-blocks saveDraft
findings.whyItBreaks: canProceed is a shared proceed gate. The new conjunct order.payment === "paid" is a legitimate submit precondition, but saveDraft also reads the same predicate. Substituting an unpaid draft {state:"draft", payment:"missing"}: canProceed is now false, so saveDraft returns "blocked". Previously state!=="ready" was enough and saveDraft returned "saved". payment "missing" is a first-class Order value; persisting an unpaid draft is a distinct action this payment check should not govern.

findings.title: Stop gating saveDraft on payment via shared canProceed
findings.whyItBreaks: canProceed now returns false whenever payment is not "paid". saveDraft shares that predicate, so a draft with payment "missing" (state="draft") that previously saved now hits if (!canProceed(order)) and returns "blocked". Payment is a legitimate submit precondition, not a save-draft precondition.

findings.title: Don't require payment on saveDraft via shared canProceed
findings.whyItBreaks: canProceed now returns order.state !== "ready" && order.payment === "paid". saveDraft (src/actions.ts:9) and submitOrder (src/actions.ts:4) both read that shared flag. Substituting payment="missing" with state="draft": canProceed is false, so saveDraft returns "blocked" instead of "saved". Saving a draft is independently valid without payment; the new conjunct over-blocks that action. submitOrder is a legitimate consumer of the payment gate; saveDraft is not.

findings.title: Publish snapshot files from stable instead of channel HEAD
findings.whyItBreaks: publishSnapshot still sets Snapshot.commit to repo.headCommit(channel) and Snapshot.channel to the requested channel, but files are now repo.filesAt(repo.headCommit("stable")). For any channel other than "stable" (including DEFAULT_CHANNEL "main"), the published file list is from a different ref than the advertised commit. Callers of this exported API receive an internally inconsistent snapshot and will publish/serve the wrong tree while believing it is channel HEAD.

findings.title: Keep snapshot files at the advertised channel commit
findings.whyItBreaks: publishSnapshot(repo, channel) still records commit=repo.headCommit(channel) and channel as given, but files are now repo.filesAt(repo.headCommit("stable")). Any channel other than stable therefore ships a commit SHA that does not contain the listed files. Callers that trust Snapshot.commit as the tree for Snapshot.files will publish, cache, or verify the wrong contents.

findings.title: Publish snapshot files from 'stable', not the channel commit
findings.whyItBreaks: publishSnapshot still sets Snapshot.commit to repo.headCommit(channel) and Snapshot.channel to the requested channel, but files are now repo.filesAt(repo.headCommit("stable")). For any channel other than "stable" — including DEFAULT_CHANNEL "main" — the returned snapshot advertises one commit and ships another commit's tree. Callers that persist or deploy Snapshot.files while treating Snapshot.commit as the source of truth publish the wrong contents. Previously files were repo.filesAt(head), so commit and files matched.

findings.title: Honor build(limit) instead of ignoring it
findings.whyItBreaks: Public build(prefix, limit=10) promises callers can cap how many items are produced. The body never reads limit and always loops range(max_count) with max_count=10, so build('x', limit=3) and build('x', limit=100) both still return 10 items. Default-path callers are unchanged; any non-default limit is silently ignored.

findings.title: Honor build()'s new limit parameter in the loop bound
findings.whyItBreaks: The public signature build(prefix, limit=10) promises the result is capped to `limit`. The body never reads `limit` and always iterates `range(max_count)` with `max_count = 10`, so build('x', limit=3) still returns 10 items. Default-path callers are unchanged (10==10), but any caller that passes a non-default limit gets the wrong length; that is the contract the new parameter ships.

findings.title: Wire unused build(limit) into the loop bound
findings.whyItBreaks: The public signature adds limit=10, which promises to cap how many prefixed items are returned. The body still sets max_count = 10 and iterates range(max_count), never reading limit. build("x", limit=3) therefore returns 10 items, same as the default; callers cannot distinguish a respected cap from the hardcoded length.

findings.title: Reject non-positive values in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: The public symbol parse_positive_int promises a positive integer (validation that changes the result). The body is still return int(value), so 0 and negatives pass. charge trusts that result and does n * 100 with no further check, so charge(-5) returns -500 and total_cents includes that in the billed sum.

findings.title: Enforce positivity in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: The public name parse_positive_int promises to parse and reject non-positive values, but the body is still return int(value). charge() (and therefore total_cents()) skip any positivity check and will convert 0 to 0 and negatives to negative cents (e.g. amount -1 → -100).

findings.title: Enforce positivity in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: The public name parse_positive_int promises the value is a positive integer, but the body is still `return int(value)`. Zero and negatives parse successfully. charge() trusts that result and does n * 100 with no further check, so charge(-1) returns -100 and total_cents([-1, 2]) returns 100 instead of rejecting the bad amount.

findings.title: Restore copy so apply_values does not mutate caller frames
findings.whyItBreaks: apply_values previously copied the input, wrote mapped values on the copy, and returned that new frame, so callers kept their original data. The function now does df.loc[df['key'] == key, 'value'] = value on the argument itself and returns that same object. Any caller that reuses, shares, or later inspects the input DataFrame will see overwritten 'value' cells; pandas-style transforms that return a frame are also expected not to mutate unless inplace is explicit.

findings.title: Keep apply_values from mutating the caller's DataFrame
findings.whyItBreaks: apply_values previously copied the input and wrote mapped values on that copy, so the caller's DataFrame was unchanged. It now assigns through df.loc and returns df, so every alias of the input is overwritten. Callers that reuse the original frame for comparison, further transforms, or shared pipeline state observe mutated values; if df is a view, the write can also leak into a parent frame.

findings.title: Do not mutate the caller DataFrame in apply_values
findings.whyItBreaks: apply_values previously copied the frame (`result = df.copy()`) and wrote mapped values only on that copy. It now does `df.loc[df["key"] == key, "value"] = value` and returns `df`, so pandas in-place assignment mutates the caller's object. Any caller that reuses the input after the call, compares identity, or passed a view/slice now observes changed `value` cells (or a SettingWithCopy miss) instead of an isolated result.

findings.title: Enforce positivity in parse_positive_int or drop the name
findings.whyItBreaks: The public rename to parse_positive_int promises a positive integer, but the body is still s.parse().unwrap_or(0), which returns negatives, zero, and maps parse errors to 0. charge() multiplies that result by 100 with no further check, so charge("-5") yields -500 and charge("abc") yields 0, the same as a real zero amount.

findings.title: Honor parse_positive_int: reject non-positive and unparseable input
findings.whyItBreaks: The public symbol was renamed to parse_positive_int, which promises to parse a positive integer (validation/filtering). The body is still `s.parse().unwrap_or(0)`: negatives pass through, 0 is returned, and unparseable input is also 0. charge() is a relying caller — it does `n * 100` with no positivity check — so charge("-5") is -500 and charge("abc") is 0, indistinguishable from a real zero amount.

findings.title: Implement the positive-int contract parse_positive_int advertises
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported symbol was renamed from read_int to parse_positive_int, which promises a positive integer result (n > 0, and a successful parse). The body is still s.parse().unwrap_or(0): negatives parse through (parse_positive_int("-1") == -1), zero is accepted, and any parse error becomes 0. charge() at src/parse.rs:6 trusts that helper and does n * 100 with no further check, so charge("-1") == -100 and charge("abc") == 0 — callers cannot tell a failed parse from a real zero, and negative amounts are billed.

findings.title: Use dbg!(&items); dbg!(items) moves the Vec
findings.whyItBreaks: dbg!($val) matches on $val by value and returns it. Vec<String> is not Copy, the macro result is discarded, and items is moved/dropped. The next line items.len() is a use of a moved value, so this public function does not compile.

findings.title: Do not move items in dbg! before items.len()
findings.whyItBreaks: std::dbg! evaluates its argument by value and returns it. The trailing semicolon drops that return, so `items` is moved. `items.len()` is then a use of a moved `Vec<String>` (E0382). Public `process` does not compile.

findings.title: Pass items by reference into dbg! so process still compiles
findings.whyItBreaks: dbg!(expr) takes ownership of expr, debug-prints it, and returns it. The return is discarded, so the Vec<String> is moved and dropped. items is not Copy, so items.len() is a use of a moved value and the public process path fails to compile.

findings.title: Compute changedPaths from pinned fromRevision, not latest
findings.whyItBreaks: Changeset.fromRevision is documented as the revision changedPaths were computed against, and consumers replay those paths on exactly that revision. buildChangeset still sets fromRevision to store.resolve(pinnedTag) but now calls store.readChangedPaths(store.resolve("latest")). Callers therefore replay a latest-based path list on top of the pinned revision: if readChangedPaths(rev) means changes since rev, the list is empty (nothing since latest) and pin-to-latest edits are skipped; if it means paths at rev, latest's paths are applied onto the pin. Either way the returned changeset is internally inconsistent and the pinnedTag argument no longer controls the path set.

findings.title: Compute changedPaths against fromRevision, not latest
findings.whyItBreaks: Changeset.fromRevision is documented as the revision changedPaths were computed against, and consumers replay those paths on exactly that revision. buildChangeset still sets fromRevision to store.resolve(pinnedTag) but now calls readChangedPaths(store.resolve("latest")). When those tags resolve to different revisions, the returned changeset is internally inconsistent: replay applies latest's path set onto the pinned revision (typically missing pin→head changes if readChangedPaths means 'since this rev', or applying the wrong snapshot if it means 'at this rev').

findings.title: Compute changedPaths from the pinned revision, not latest
findings.whyItBreaks: Changeset.fromRevision is documented as the revision changedPaths were computed against, and consumers replay onto exactly that revision. fromRevision is still store.resolve(pinnedTag), but changedPaths is now store.readChangedPaths(store.resolve("latest")). When the pin is not latest, the returned path list is not the delta from fromRevision (typically empty if latest is HEAD, or a different snapshot otherwise). Replay therefore no-ops or applies the wrong files on top of the pinned revision.

findings.whyItBreaks: 0002 renames users.email to contact_email. src/query.sql is unchanged and still runs SELECT email FROM users, so after this migration the only application query fails with a missing-column error.

findings.title: Rename users.email without updating SELECT email query
findings.whyItBreaks: 0002 renames users.email to contact_email. src/query.sql still runs SELECT email FROM users, so the only application read path errors with a missing-column failure as soon as the migration applies.

findings.title: Update query still selecting users.email after column rename

findings.title: Serialize reserve; do not await between stock check and decrement
findings.whyItBreaks: reserve reads remaining and admits the reservation, then awaits store.save before writing stock. In JavaScript that await yields, so a second reserve() started before the first continues (Promise.all, two requests, or a missing await) still sees the old Map value. Both pass remaining <= 0, both call save(remaining - 1), both return true. With stock=1 this reserves two units, and both writes persist 0 (lost update for any remaining > 1). The pre-await body was a single synchronous critical section and could not interleave.

findings.title: Decrement stock before awaiting save to prevent oversell
findings.whyItBreaks: reserve() reads this.stock, then awaits store.save before writing remaining-1. The original sync method could not interleave; the new await yields. Two overlapping reserve() calls on the same SKU both observe the same remaining, both persist remaining-1, both set that value, and both return true. With stock=1, both reservations succeed and the map/store end at 0 instead of rejecting the second call.

findings.title: Decrement stock before awaiting save to prevent oversell
findings.whyItBreaks: reserve is now async and awaits store.save before this.stock.set. In JS, that await is a yield: two overlapping reserve(sku) calls both read the same remaining, both pass remaining <= 0, both persist remaining-1 (last-write-wins, not a delta), both return true. Example: load('sku', 1) then Promise.all([reserve, reserve]) succeeds twice and store/memory settle at 0 instead of rejecting the second call. Base reserve() was synchronous, so the read-check-decrement could not interleave.

findings.title: Stop multiplying retry sleep by 1000 after backoff switched to ms
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff() previously returned seconds capped at 30. This PR returns milliseconds capped at 30_000, and schedulePoll was updated to pass that value straight to setTimeout. retry.ts is unchanged and still does sleep(backoff(a) * 1000), where sleep already takes milliseconds. Substitution: backoff(0)=1000 → sleep(1_000_000 ms) (16.7 min, was 1s); backoff(5)=30000 → sleep(30_000_000 ms) (8.3h, was 30s). Every failed retry waits 1000× too long.

findings.title: Do not multiply retry sleep by 1000 after backoff returns ms
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff() changed from seconds capped at 30 to milliseconds capped at 30_000 (attempt 0 → 1000, later attempts → 30000). poll.ts was updated to pass that value straight to setTimeout, but retry.ts still does sleep(backoff(a) * 1000) while sleep already takes ms. First retry waits 1_000_000 ms (~16.7 min) instead of 1 s; capped attempts wait 30_000_000 ms (~8.3 h) instead of 30 s, so job retries stall.

findings.title: Drop leftover *1000 in retry after backoff returns milliseconds
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff() changed from seconds (cap 30) to milliseconds (cap 30_000). schedulePoll was updated to pass backoff(attempt) straight to setTimeout, but the other in-repo caller still does sleep(backoff(a) * 1000) while sleep already takes ms. Substituting the new values: attempt 0 waits 1_000_000ms (was 1000ms); the cap waits 30_000_000ms / ~8.3h (was 30s). Job retries stall for hours instead of seconds.

findings.title: Propagate File.Close error instead of defer-ignoring it
findings.whyItBreaks: Save is an exported write path. The previous success path returned f.Close() after a successful Flush, so Close failures (EIO/ENOSPC/NFS delayed write) reached the caller as a non-nil error. The new body defers f.Close() (error ignored) and returns only w.Flush(); when Flush succeeds and Close fails, Save returns nil and callers treat a failed write as success.

findings.title: Propagate f.Close error instead of discarding it
findings.whyItBreaks: Base Save returned f.Close() after a successful Flush, so a close/writeback failure (ENOSPC, NFS, etc.) was reported as a failed save. Head always defers f.Close() (error discarded) and returns only w.Flush(); if Flush succeeds, Save returns nil even when Close fails. Save is exported and has no in-repo callers, so every consumer is forced to conflate close failure with a completed write.

findings.title: Propagate Save's file Close error instead of discarding it
findings.whyItBreaks: Base Save returned f.Close() after a successful Flush, so close-time write failures (ENOSPC/EIO on some filesystems, delayed writeback) were visible to callers. Head installs defer f.Close() (error ignored) and returns only w.Flush(). Flush succeeding then Close failing now yields nil, so callers cannot distinguish a completed save from a close failure and may treat the file as durably written. Save is exported; there are no in-repo callers, but the public error contract itself now conflates failure with success.

findings.title: Stop dropping the last row of each page window
findings.whyItBreaks: `_window_bounds` returns a Python half-open [start, end) (end = min(start+page_size, row_count)). The old loop used range(start, end) and included every row in the page. The new loop uses range(start, end - 1), so index end-1 is never collected. Substitution: rows=['a','b','c','d','e'], page_size=2 → page 0 bounds (0,2) yields ['a'] not ['a','b']; page 1 bounds (2,4) yields ['c'] not ['c','d']; page 2 bounds (4,5) yields [] not ['e']. render_page/summarize therefore omit the last item of every page, skip display numbers, and emit an empty last page whenever the remainder is 1.

findings.title: Stop dropping the last row of every page_window
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds returns half-open [start, end) (end = min(start+page_size, row_count)). Python range is also half-open, so range(start, end - 1) yields [start, end-1) and omits the last index of every page. Concrete: rows=['a','b','c','d','e'], page_size=2 → page 0 is ['a'] not ['a','b']; page 2 (remainder 1) is [] not ['e']. page_size=1 yields an empty window for every page. render_page and summarize inherit the missing rows.

findings.title: Stop excluding the last row from each page_window
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds returns a half-open [start, end) (end = min(start+page_size, row_count)). page_window then loops range(start, end - 1), so index end-1 is never yielded. A full page of size N returns N-1 rows; a remainder or page_size=1 page (start+1==end) returns []. render_page/summarize therefore omit the last item of every page and emit blank remainder pages. Example: rows=['a','b','c','d','e'], page_size=2 → windows [['a'],['c'],[]] instead of [['a','b'],['c','d'],['e']].

findings.title: Fix inverted TTL check that serves expired values and drops live ones
findings.whyItBreaks: get() used to return a hit when age < ttlMs and delete on expiry. The comparison was flipped to age > ttlMs, so a live entry (age < ttlMs) falls through to delete+null, and an expired entry is returned as a hit. Immediate get-after-set misses; stale values are served after TTL. Equality (age === ttlMs) still expires, so this is not an inclusive-bound tweak.

findings.title: Don't splice in forEach; consecutive done jobs survive pruneDone
findings.whyItBreaks: filter(!done) removed every done job and returned a new array. forEach + splice(index,1) mutates while the cursor advances: removing index i shifts i+1 into i, then forEach visits i+1 and skips that shifted job. Input [{done:true},{done:true},{done:false}] becomes [{done:true},{done:false}] — a done job remains. Same skip for any adjacent done pair. Also mutates the caller's array in place (same reference returned).

findings.title: Restore TTL comparison so fresh entries hit and expired miss
findings.whyItBreaks: TtlCache.get used to return a value while age < ttlMs and otherwise evict. The predicate is now age > ttlMs, so a just-written entry (age ≈ 0) takes the else branch, is deleted, and returns null; an expired entry is returned as a hit. The public get() contract is inverted.

findings.title: Do not splice the job list inside forEach in pruneDone
findings.whyItBreaks: forEach captures length up front and visits incrementing indexes. splice(index,1) shifts later jobs left, so a done job that lands on an already-visited index is never seen (e.g. [done, done, pending] becomes [done, pending]). The previous filter returned a new array of all not-done jobs; this also mutates the caller’s array in place, so leftover done jobs remain on the original list.

findings.title: Restore TtlCache freshness comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: get used to return a value while age < ttlMs and evict otherwise. The operator was flipped to `>`; immediately after set, age is ~0 so `0 > ttlMs` is false for any positive TTL, so the live entry is deleted and get returns null. Once age exceeds ttlMs the same branch returns the expired value. The public cache is inverted: fresh misses, stale hits.

findings.title: Do not splice the job array while forEach iterates
findings.whyItBreaks: filter removed every done job and returned a new array. forEach captures length up front and then increments the index after each callback; splice(index, 1) shifts the next element into the current index, so that element is never visited. Input [done, done, active] becomes [done, active]. The function also mutates the caller's array in place, which the previous implementation did not.

findings.title: Guard averageAmount against empty input to avoid NaN
findings.whyItBreaks: The empty-array early return was removed. reduce(..., 0) on [] is 0, then total/rows.length is 0/0, which is NaN in JS. Callers that previously got 0 now poison arithmetic, equality (NaN !== NaN), and JSON (JSON.stringify(NaN) is null).

findings.title: Copy rows before sorting in busiest
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort mutates in place and returns the same array. Dropping `[...rows]` means busiest(rows) reorders the caller's data by amount, so later iteration, display, or persistence of that array no longer matches the order the caller passed.

findings.title: Restore empty-array guard in averageAmount to avoid NaN
findings.whyItBreaks: averageAmount previously returned 0 for []. The guard is gone, so reduce yields 0 and `0 / 0` is NaN. That is a public-API behavior change: callers that treated empty input as a finite mean now get a value that fails every comparison and poisons later arithmetic/JSON (JSON.stringify(NaN) === 'null').

findings.title: Copy rows before sorting in busiest to avoid mutating callers
findings.whyItBreaks: busiest used to rank a shallow copy (`[...rows].sort`). It now calls `rows.sort`, which mutates the input in place. Any caller that reuses `rows` after this query (table order, later stats, identity of `rows[0]`) observes a reordered array even though the function is a read of the max-amount row.

findings.title: Return 0 for empty averageAmount instead of NaN
findings.whyItBreaks: The empty-array guard was removed. reduce on [] with initializer 0 yields 0, then 0 / 0 is NaN. The exported function previously returned 0; callers that display, persist, or do arithmetic on the result now get a poisoning NaN (JSON null, every comparison false).

findings.title: Copy before sort so busiest does not mutate caller rows
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort mutates in place. Dropping `[...rows]` reorders the caller’s array, so later iteration, display, or persistence of that same list no longer matches the original order. The previous implementation copied first; the return value is unchanged, but caller-owned data is not.

findings.title: Restore numeric sort; default sort ranks scores as strings
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort() with no comparefn stringifies elements and orders UTF-16, then reverse() only flips that string order. Base used (a,b)=>b-a (numeric descending). For players A=9,B=10,C=8 and n=1: default sort yields [10,8,9], reverse yields [9,8,10], cutoff=scores[0]=9, filter score>=9 keeps A then B, slice(0,1) returns A (9) instead of B (10). Any mixed digit-length or signed scores mis-rank; same-digit positives can coincidentally look correct.

findings.title: Restore numeric descending sort in rankScores
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.prototype.sort() with no compareFn orders by ToString (UTF-16), not by numeric value. rankScores then reverse()s that lexicographic order and topPlayers takes scores[n-1] as the cutoff. For players [{a,20},{b,100},{c,3}] and n=1: sort() yields [100,20,3], reverse() yields [3,20,100], cutoff is 3, filter keeps everyone, slice(0,1) returns a/20 instead of b/100. Same failure for any mixed digit-length scores (the common 10 vs 2 vs 100 case). formatBoard inherits the wrong set.

findings.title: Use a numeric comparator when ranking scores
findings.whyItBreaks: rankScores replaced scores.sort((a, b) => b - a) with scores.sort() then reverse(). Array.prototype.sort() with no comparefn stringifies elements and orders UTF-16 code units, so mixed-magnitude scores are not numeric-descending. topPlayers then reads cutoff at index n-1 of that array and keeps p.score >= cutoff, so the exported top-N set is wrong. Example: players [{a,1},{b,2},{c,10}] with n=2 ranks as [2,10,1], cutoff=10, and returns only c; numeric ranking is [10,2,1], cutoff=2, and must return b and c (original order). formatBoard inherits the same wrong list.

findings.title: Restore constant-time HMAC comparison in verify
findings.whyItBreaks: verify() is the webhook auth gate. Replacing hmac.compare_digest with str == lets CPython short-circuit on the first mismatched hex nibble, so an attacker who can measure handle()/verify() latency can recover given_signature against the expected HMAC and forge payloads that processor() then accepts.

findings.title: Restore constant-time HMAC comparison in verify()
findings.whyItBreaks: verify() is the only auth gate for handle(): a matching signature runs processor(payload); a mismatch returns 401. hmac.compare_digest was replaced with CPython str == str, which short-circuits on the first differing byte. An attacker who can measure verify/handle latency can recover the expected 64-char hex HMAC byte-by-byte and then forge webhooks, so attacker-controlled payloads are processed as authenticated.

findings.title: Restore constant-time HMAC signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: verify() is the only auth gate for handle(): a matching signature runs processor(payload); a mismatch returns 401. Replacing hmac.compare_digest with str == makes comparison short-circuit on the first mismatched hex character of the SHA-256 HMAC. An attacker who can measure handle/verify latency can recover the expected digest character-by-character and then forge webhooks. hmac.compare_digest exists specifically to prevent that side channel and was the previous implementation.

findings.title: Keep balance updates inside the transfer transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: Base transfer() applied the ledger INSERT and both account UPDATEs inside one `with db.transaction()` so a later failure rolled all three back. Head still commits `_record_ledger` at the end of that block, then calls `_apply_balances` at the same indent as `with`. Any exception or crash in the debit/credit UPDATEs leaves a committed ledger row with unchanged balances; if statements autocommit, a failure on the credit UPDATE also debits the source without crediting the destination.

findings.title: Keep ledger and balance updates in one transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: Base `transfer()` ran the ledger INSERT and both account UPDATEs inside one `db.transaction()`. Head still opens that transaction but only `_record_ledger` is inside it; `_apply_balances` is dedented to the function body, so the ledger row commits when the `with` exits and the two UPDATEs then run outside that transaction (and not atomically with each other). A crash or exception in `_apply_balances` after commit leaves a recorded transfer with unchanged balances; if the debit UPDATE succeeds and the credit UPDATE fails, `from_acct` is reduced with no corresponding credit to `to_acct`.

findings.title: Keep ledger and balance updates in one transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously the ledger INSERT and both account UPDATEs ran inside one `with db.transaction():` block, so they committed or rolled back together. The refactor still commits `_record_ledger` in that block, then calls `_apply_balances` after the context exits. A crash or exception during either UPDATE leaves a committed ledger row with balances not fully applied; if only the debit UPDATE succeeds, cents leave `from_acct` and never reach `to_acct`. The two UPDATEs are also no longer atomic with each other.

findings.title: Restore UTC getters in billingDay; local TZ changes day keys
findings.whyItBreaks: billingDay previously returned YYYY-MM-DD from getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate. It now uses getFullYear/getMonth/getDate, so the string is the host's local calendar date. sameBillingDay (line 8) compares those strings: two instants on the same UTC day that straddle local midnight become unequal (and the reverse). Example: at TZ=America/New_York, new Date('2026-08-31T03:00:00.000Z') was '2026-08-31' and is now '2026-08-30'. Hosts in different zones, or DST boundaries, emit different keys for the same instant; persisted UTC day keys stop matching.

findings.title: Restore UTC getters in billingDay
findings.whyItBreaks: billingDay previously built YYYY-MM-DD from getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate, so a given Date instant always produced the same key. The refactor keeps pad() but reads getFullYear/getMonth/getDate, which are the host local calendar. For 2026-01-01T00:30:00.000Z in America/New_York that returns 2025-12-31 instead of 2026-01-01. sameBillingDay then classifies two UTC-same-day instants as different days (and two local-same-day instants that straddle UTC midnight as the same day). There is no timezone argument, so this is process TZ, not a customer TZ; any persisted/idempotent billing-day key computed under UTC will mismatch after deploy.

findings.title: Compute billingDay with UTC date parts, not local
findings.whyItBreaks: billingDay previously returned a timezone-stable UTC YYYY-MM-DD. It now uses getFullYear/getMonth/getDate, so the same instant is a different billing day on hosts whose local date differs from UTC (near midnight, DST, non-UTC servers). Example: 2026-01-01T03:00:00.000Z is 2026-01-01 in UTC but 2025-12-31 in America/New_York. sameBillingDay therefore treats a same-UTC-day pair as different (or a cross-UTC-midnight pair as the same), which breaks day identity, lookups, and any persisted day key written under the old contract.

findings.title: Restore tenant in the profile memo key
findings.whyItBreaks: Module-level `memo` is now keyed only by `account`. After `readProfile(t1, acct, …)` caches a hit, `readProfile(t2, acct, …)` returns t1's Profile (including `tenant`/`displayName`) and never calls `fetchProfile(t2, acct)`. The reverse `memo.set` also overwrites t1's entry with t2's. `readProfile` is exported and still takes `tenant` as a required identity argument.

findings.title: Keep tenant in the profile memo key
findings.whyItBreaks: memo is a process-wide Map. key is now only account, but fetchProfile still loads by (tenant, account) and Profile is tenant-scoped. After readProfile('t1','alice', ...) caches, readProfile('t2','alice', ...) hits memo.get(account) and returns t1's Profile without calling fetchProfile; memo.set then overwrites t1's entry with t2's.

findings.title: Restore tenant in the profile memo key
findings.whyItBreaks: The shared module-level memo is now keyed only by `account` while `fetchProfile` remains tenant-scoped. After `readProfile('t1','alice', …)` stores under `'alice'`, `readProfile('t2','alice', …)` hits that entry and returns t1's Profile (`tenant`, `displayName`) without calling fetch. `memo.set` also overwrites the slot, so whichever tenant populates last poisons the other. Account IDs are not globally unique (`Profile` still has both `tenant` and `account`; the previous key was `${tenant}:${account}`).

findings.title: Preserve missing-key errors instead of returning empty string
findings.whyItBreaks: load() previously threw Error(`missing: ${key}`) when Map.get returned undefined, which is distinct from a stored empty string (Map.get("") is ""). The new catch-all returns "" for that throw (and any other exception). Callers of load and loadAll can no longer tell a missing key from a real empty value, and loadAll no longer fail-fasts: keys.map(load) now inserts "" for missing keys instead of propagating. This is an exported public swallow, so the unusable contract is the defect even aside from the in-repo loadAll caller.

findings.title: Do not swallow missing-key errors as empty strings in load
findings.whyItBreaks: load() previously threw Error(`missing: ${key}`) when store.get returned undefined. The new catch-all returns "", a legitimate Map value, so callers cannot tell a missing key (or any other throw) from a stored empty string. loadAll maps load() and therefore now returns an array of holes instead of aborting; both functions are exported, so the public contract itself forces failure-as-value.

findings.title: Do not swallow missing-key errors as empty strings
findings.whyItBreaks: load() previously threw Error(`missing: ${key}`) when store.get returned undefined, and that exception propagated to loadAll (keys.map) and to any external caller of the exported function. The new catch-all returns "". "" is a legitimate Map<string, string> value, so callers cannot tell a missing key (or a TypeError from a bad store) from a real empty entry. loadAll no longer fail-fasts: a missing key becomes a silent "" slot in the returned array. The catch is not limited to the missing-key throw; it also downgrades any exception from store.get.

findings.title: Rethrow last error when retryBackground exhausts retries
findings.whyItBreaks: retryBackground is a new exported wrapper. It catches every exception from fn with an empty handler, then returns normally when retries run out or Date.now() exceeds the deadline. Success (fn() then return), retry exhaustion (fall off the loop), and timeout (early return) all yield void, so callers are forced to treat failure as success: they cannot error, retry at a higher layer, or avoid persisting/reporting a completed job.

findings.title: Propagate retryBackground failures instead of swallowing them
findings.whyItBreaks: New exported retryBackground returns void and never rethrows. An empty catch (lines 27-29) discards every exception from fn(); after retries are exhausted the function falls through with a normal return; on deadline it returns at line 23. Success, timeout, and total failure are the same observable result (undefined), so a caller that treats return as 'work completed' will proceed after fn() never succeeded. That is the public contract shipping now; there are no in-repo callers, which does not clear a public swallow.

findings.title: Coerce Field value before reading .length
findings.whyItBreaks: FieldProps.value is now string | number, but the body reads value.length. Numbers have no length, so a caller passing a number (the new public contract) gets defaultValue "len=undefined" instead of a digit count. Exported Field/FieldProps is the contract even with no in-repo callers.

findings.title: Coerce Field value to string before reading length
findings.whyItBreaks: FieldProps.value is now string | number, but the body reads value.length. Numbers have no length, so a numeric value (including 0) yields undefined and the input's defaultValue becomes "len=undefined" instead of a digit/character length. The exported type promises numbers are valid inputs; the rendered result does not implement that.

findings.title: Don't read .length on string|number Field value
findings.whyItBreaks: FieldProps.value was widened to string | number, but the body interpolates value.length. Numbers have no length; a caller passing 42 gets defaultValue "len=undefined" instead of a length. This is the public Field contract: the new union promises numbers work, and the observed input value is wrong.

findings.title: Stop echoing secrets.TOKEN into GitHub Actions logs
findings.whyItBreaks: The added step assigns ${{ secrets.TOKEN }} to TOKEN and interpolates it into stdout (`echo "deploying with $TOKEN"`). Workflow logs persist and are readable by anyone with Actions log access (world-readable on public repos). GitHub log redaction is a literal-string filter: it misses secrets shorter than the mask threshold, multiline/structured values, and any transformed output, so the deploy credential can appear in cleartext. TOKEN is also step-scoped to this echo and is not passed to `make build`, so the leak is not even required for the subsequent build.

findings.title: Do not echo secrets.TOKEN into GitHub Actions logs
findings.whyItBreaks: The added step assigns secrets.TOKEN to env TOKEN and interpolates it in echo "deploying with $TOKEN". That writes the deploy credential to the step's stdout, which GitHub Actions persists in job logs for every push. Log redaction is best-effort (it misses short, structured, whitespace-bearing, or later-transformed values) and is bypassable, so the secret can appear in logs visible to anyone with Actions read access — or to the public if the repo is public. The env is step-scoped and is not passed to `make build`, so the only effect of this change is logging the secret.

findings.title: Stop echoing secrets.TOKEN to GitHub Actions logs
findings.whyItBreaks: The added step sets TOKEN from ${{ secrets.TOKEN }} and runs echo "deploying with $TOKEN", so every push writes the deploy credential to that step's stdout. GitHub log redaction only exact-matches registered secret values (plus a few encodings) and is documented as best-effort, not a boundary: short or structured secrets, debug/diagnostic dumps, and any later transformation are not reliably masked. Actions logs are readable by anyone with log access (public on a public repo). TOKEN is never passed to `make build`, so the step's only effect is putting the secret on the log path.

findings.title: Restore git spawnSync maxBuffer; 1MiB default fails large PR diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync default maxBuffer is 1024*1024. git() is the helper that captures `git diff mergeBase headSha` (the full PR patch). Diffs above 1MiB kill the child (status null, ENOBUFS); git() treats that as failure and runGithub's catch posts a failed check and sets exitCode=1. PRs that previously fit in the explicit 64MiB cap (lockfiles, generated files, moderate-to-large source diffs) now error instead of reviewing. gh/ghText still use 64MiB; only git() lost it.

findings.title: Restore 64MiB maxBuffer on git spawnSync
findings.whyItBreaks: Omitting maxBuffer makes spawnSync use Node's default 1MiB. git() captures the full PR patch via `git diff mergeBase headSha`; when that stdout exceeds 1MiB the child is killed (ENOBUFS / status null), `res.status !== 0` throws, and runGithub never reaches review(). Those git() calls sit outside the later try/catch, so the job dies before posting the 'review failed' check. gh()/ghText() still pass 64MiB, so this is an accidental drop of the git-specific allowance.

findings.title: Restore git() maxBuffer; 1MiB default fails large PR patches
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync from node:child_process defaults maxBuffer to 1024*1024. git() is the path that loads the full PR patch via git diff mergeBase headSha; gh/ghText still pass 64MiB, so this drop is inconsistent. When stdout exceeds 1MiB, spawnSync kills the child (ENOBUFS, status null), git() treats status!==0 as failure and throws, and runGithub's catch posts a failure check and sets exitCode=1. Large but previously-reviewable PRs (lockfile/generated diffs) now fail the review job.

findings.title: Set bundle.baseSha to mergeBase, not PR_BASE_SHA
findings.whyItBreaks: baseSha is process.env.PR_BASE_SHA || merge-base(origin/main, HEAD). GitHub Actions typically sets PR_BASE_SHA to pull_request.base.sha (tip of the base branch), which is not an ancestor of head when the PR is behind. mergeBase = git merge-base(baseSha, headSha) is the actual fork point. patch and changedFiles still use mergeBase, but Bundle.baseSha is now the pre-merge-base value (ES6 shorthand of the wrong binding). Any review consumer that treats bundle.baseSha as the left side of the comparison (git diff/show against base) reviews main-since-fork plus the PR, not the PR. The two SHAs coincide only when PR_BASE_SHA is already an ancestor of headSha.

findings.title: Pin Codex exec sandbox back to read-only
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous argv pinned `-s read-only`, which Codex treats as a CLI flag (highest precedence) and therefore overrode `sandbox_mode` from `$CODEX_HOME/config.toml` and project `.codex/config.toml`. After this deletion, `--sandbox` defaults to configuration. `codex exec` is non-interactive (no approval prompts) and `spawnSync` uses `cwd: opts.repoPath`. A common `sandbox_mode = "workspace-write"` (or `danger-full-access`) then lets the spawned agent mutate the target repo—or the host—during a run whose only contract is returning `--output-last-message`. Nothing else in this diff needs write access.

findings.title: Restore the pinned read-only Codex sandbox
findings.whyItBreaks: runCodex previously pinned `codex exec` to `-s read-only` while spawning with cwd=opts.repoPath. That flag is removed with no replacement. `codex exec` never prompts for approval, so sandbox mode is the only write/exec control. Without the explicit pin, mode falls through to the operator's Codex config/CLI default (commonly workspace-write on trusted local repos). The agent can then edit files and run mutating commands inside the repository under review.

findings.title: Restore Codex exec -s read-only sandbox pin
findings.whyItBreaks: runCodex previously passed `-s read-only` to `codex exec`, which is a CLI override and therefore wins over `$CODEX_HOME/config.toml` and trusted-project `.codex/config.toml`. After this deletion the argv has no sandbox flag. Upstream `codex exec` sets `sandbox_mode` only from that CLI arg (otherwise `None`) while hardcoding `approval_policy: Never`. On a typical developer machine `sandbox_mode` is `workspace-write` or `danger-full-access`; combined with never-approval and `cwd: opts.repoPath`, the model can write files and run commands in the reviewed tree with no prompt. Exec's documented default of read-only only applies when config also omits sandbox_mode, so this is not a no-op.

findings.title: Restore merge-base when computing the PR patch
findings.whyItBreaks: The old path computed mergeBase=git merge-base(baseSha, headSha) and then diffed mergeBase..headSha. That is a no-op only when PR_BASE_SHA is already an ancestor of the PR tip. PR_BASE_SHA overrides a merge-base fallback, so the live override path is a SHA that need not be an ancestor (the usual GitHub Actions value is pull_request.base.sha, the base-branch tip). git diff baseSha HEAD is then a two-dot diff: it includes reverse patches for commits that landed on the base after the branch diverged. changedFileSet(cwd, baseSha) uses the same left side (git diff --name-only baseSha HEAD), so changedPaths and bundle.changedFiles also include files the PR did not change. review(bundle) therefore analyzes the wrong scope; inlineComments can emit paths/lines that are not in the GitHub PR three-dot diff, which trips the existing review-API catch and posts a body-only review. The right-hand side also switched from headSha (PR_HEAD_SHA || rev-parse HEAD) to the symbolic ref HEAD while postReview still sends commit_id=headSha, so a merge-commit checkout no longer matches the commit the comments are attached to.

findings.title: Restore merge-base..headSha for the PR patch and file set
findings.whyItBreaks: headSha is process.env.PR_HEAD_SHA || HEAD and baseSha is process.env.PR_BASE_SHA || merge-base(origin/main, HEAD). The old code then computed mergeBase=merge-base(baseSha, headSha) and used git diff mergeBase headSha (GitHub 3-dot PR range). The new code uses git diff baseSha HEAD and changedFileSet(cwd, baseSha), which is git diff --name-only baseSha HEAD. Substituting the env-var path: if PR_BASE_SHA is the base-branch tip (pull_request.base.sha) rather than the fork point, the 2-dot tree diff includes reverse changes for commits unique to main and drops PR files whose final tree matches main. Those paths feed changedPaths.has at inlineComments (L63), so comments are attached to files GitHub does not treat as part of the PR, or omitted for files the PR did change; the existing catch at L96 then republishes the review with no inline comments. Independently, if PR_HEAD_SHA != workspace HEAD (default pull_request checkout is the merge commit), bundle.patch is computed from HEAD while postReview/postCheck still send commit_id/head_sha=headSha (L85, L124, L178), so line-mapped comments target the wrong commit.

findings.title: Compute PR patch via merge-base and headSha, not HEAD
findings.whyItBreaks: runGithub is Actions-only and reads PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA. GitHub's pull_request.base.sha is the base-branch tip, which is not an ancestor of the PR head when the branch is behind. The old code used merge-base(baseSha, headSha) then git diff mergeBase headSha (three-dot / PR-files semantics). The new git diff baseSha HEAD is two-dot: it injects reverse diffs of commits that landed on the base after the fork, and changedFileSet (git diff --name-only baseSha HEAD) marks those extra paths as PR files. Those paths feed bundle.patch/changedFiles into review() and gate inline comments via changedPaths.has. The right side is also now working-tree HEAD while postReview still sends commit_id: headSha (PR_HEAD_SHA), so comment line numbers need not exist on the commit GitHub is asked to review; the existing review-create catch then drops all inline comments.

findings.title: Restore function replacers so `$` in patches stays literal
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace with a string replacement runs GetSubstitution: `$&` becomes the matched placeholder, `$``/`$'` splice the rest of the prompt, `$$` becomes `$`, and `$1`–`$9` become empty (no captures). The previous `() => value` replacers inserted the text literally. `bundle.patch` is a git diff; `JSON.stringify(bundle)` embeds that same patch. Typical JS/shell/Make hunks contain `$&`, `$1`, `$$`, and `$'`, so the review and critic prompts silently receive a mutated bundle/patch and Codex judges the wrong text.

findings.title: Pass replacer functions so replace() does not interpolate $ in patches
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace interpolates replacement strings via GetSubstitution even when the search is a literal. The previous `() => value` wrappers returned the insertion text verbatim. After this change, any `$&`, `$$`, `$`` , or `$'` in JSON.stringify(bundle), JSON.stringify(candidate), or bundle.patch is rewritten before runCodex. bundle.patch is raw git diff of source; those sequences are common (JS `$&`/`$$`, Make `$$`, bash `$'...'`). Concrete effect: template `BEGIN {{PATCH}} END` plus patch `a $& b $$ c` becomes `BEGIN a {{PATCH}} b $ c END` instead of the literal patch, so both LLM calls review corrupted input with no error.

findings.title: Restore function replacers so $ in patch/JSON is literal
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace treats a string replacement as a template (ECMA-262 GetSubstitution): $$ → $, $& → the matched placeholder, $` → text before the match, $' → text after. bundle.patch is a raw git diff and JSON.stringify(bundle|candidate) embeds that text; $ is not JSON-escaped. Real diffs routinely contain those sequences (JS .replace(..., '$&'|'$1'), shell/Make $$). The critic therefore sees a mutated patch, and the review prompt can see mutated bundle JSON. The previous () => value replacers insert the string unchanged.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of defaulting them to P1/bug
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeFinding no longer throws on invalid/missing required fields; it substitutes severity "P1", category "bug", title "Untitled finding", file "", lineStart/lineEnd 0 (or NaN for non-numeric lines), and empty whyItBreaks/suggestedFix. normalizeReview always maps through that path (strict throw-or-drop is gone), so a caller cannot tell a parse failure from a legitimate P1 bug finding. Substitutions: severity "" / "critical" → SEVERITIES.includes @98 false → "P1"; category undefined → CATEGORIES.includes @100 false → "bug"; file undefined → "" @103 (old !file threw); lineStart undefined → 0 @104 (old lineStart<=0 threw); lineStart "x" → NaN @104 (old !Number.isFinite threw). JSON.stringify(NaN) becomes null.

findings.title: Stop coercing invalid findings into real P1/bug records
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeFinding previously threw on non-object input, unknown severity/category, missing file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix, and non-positive lineStart/lineEnd. normalizeReview defaulted to strict=true, so those errors aborted the whole parse. The new body maps every failure onto a plausible Finding: invalid/missing severity → "P1", invalid category → "bug", missing title → "Untitled finding", missing file/why/fix → "", missing lines → 0, and non-numeric lines → NaN. normalizeReview always does findings.map(normalizeFinding) with the strict flag removed, so a payload that used to throw now returns findings a caller cannot tell from model-authored ones (e.g. omit severity and you persist a P1; typo a P0 and it is silently downgraded). That is a public-API swallow: failure and a real value are the same type and the same shape.

findings.title: Stop defaulting malformed findings to fabricated P1 records
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeFinding is exported and is the only findings parser (normalizeReview maps every element through it at line 131). Previously it threw on a non-object, invalid severity/category, missing file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix, or non-positive lineStart/lineEnd. It now returns a Finding with severity "P1", category "bug", title "Untitled finding", file/why/fix "", and lineStart/lineEnd 0 (or NaN if a non-numeric line is provided). Callers of the public API are forced to treat parse failure as a real P1 bug. The removed strict flag (default true) used to propagate those errors; the old strict=false path dropped invalid findings instead of materializing fakes. Empty-string title is also not replaced (?? does not catch ''), so required fields can be blank while still looking like a valid Finding.

findings.title: Restore --repo for pre-checkout gh pr view on dispatch
findings.whyItBreaks: The else branch is the live workflow_dispatch path (EVENT_HEAD is empty when there is no pull_request payload). It runs before actions/checkout, so the workspace is not this repo's git clone. gh pr view <number> without -R/--repo or GH_REPO resolves the repo from CWD git remotes only (official env docs list GH_REPO, not GITHUB_REPOSITORY; cli/cli#3556 is still open). On a clean workspace that command fails (or, on a dirty self-hosted workspace, uses leftover remotes). Checkout then never gets the PR head SHA, so the documented manual-review trigger cannot check out or review the requested PR.

findings.title: Restore repo flag on pre-checkout gh pr view
findings.whyItBreaks: The else branch is the workflow_dispatch path: EVENT_HEAD is github.event.pull_request.head.sha, which is empty on dispatch, so the job calls `gh pr view "$PR_NUM"` with no -R/--repo. That step runs before actions/checkout, so there is no local git remote. gh resolves the repo from --repo, GH_REPO, or git remotes only — it does not read GITHUB_REPOSITORY (cli/cli#3556 still open; GH_REPO is the documented env). On a clean workspace the command fails with 'not a git repository' and never writes head/base SHAs; Checkout PR head then has nothing to fetch. On this self-hosted runner a leftover .git from a prior job can make it appear to work, or bind the wrong remote. pull_request webhook runs are unaffected because EVENT_HEAD is set.

findings.title: Keep -R on gh pr view in the pre-checkout ref step
findings.whyItBreaks: The else branch is the workflow_dispatch path (EVENT_HEAD is empty because github.event.pull_request is absent). That branch runs as the first step, before actions/checkout, and now calls `gh pr view "$PR_NUM"` with no -R/--repo and no GH_REPO. gh does not read GITHUB_REPOSITORY (only GH_REPO, --repo, or cwd git remotes). In a clean GITHUB_WORKSPACE this fails with 'not a git repository' / no remotes, so head/base outputs are never set and Checkout PR head never runs. On a self-hosted runner with leftover remotes it may instead resolve the PR number against whatever repo happens to be in the workspace.

findings.title: Parse candidate strictly; do not drop malformed findings
findings.whyItBreaks: The first Codex pass is now parsed with strict=false, so normalizeReview silently filters out any malformed finding instead of failing. A real P1/P2 finding with one malformed required field is reduced to findings:[] before the critic ever sees it; the critic can only prune that empty list, and deriveVerdict then returns pass.

findings.title: Do not coerce malformed review JSON into an empty review
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview is an exported public parser. It previously threw on a non-object payload and on missing/wrong-typed summary, findings, checked, and residual_risks. Those throws are gone: null, {}, {summary: 1}, or a truncated object now return {summary:"", findings:[], checked:[], residual_risks:[]}. Empty string and empty arrays were already legitimate outputs (old code accepted summary:"" and findings:[]), so callers can no longer tell a failed/malformed model response from a real zero-finding review and will persist, score, or report the fallback as success.

findings.title: Stop mapping malformed review output to an empty successful review
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview is exported and previously threw on non-object input or missing/non-string summary / non-array findings, checked, or residual_risks. Those throws are gone: null/undefined/non-objects and incomplete objects now return {summary:"", findings:[], checked:[], residual_risks:[]}. Callers (in-repo or future) cannot tell a parse failure from a legitimate empty review and will persist or report dropped findings and dropped blocking residual_risks as a real result.
